newsitem.title: UK: EMERGING MARKET OUTLOOK-Russia,Poland spark nerves.
newsitem.headline: EMERGING MARKET OUTLOOK-Russia,Poland spark nerves.

text.p: Russia will hang heaviest over the emerging market horizon this week as investors reassess the value of its debt and equity assets, while nail-biting over Poland, Bulgaria and Mexico continues. "The situation in Russia still looks pretty unstable," said Nigel Rendell, emerging market strategist at James Capel in London.

"No one's very sure about how well Yeltsin is, and what Lebed's planning next, but on top of that comes the fact that the IMF has withheld the latest payments of its $10 million loan for Russia," he added.
"The bond and equity markets both have a big question mark hanging over them."

News that an International Monetary Fund mission had left Moscow last week without approving the loan tranche, citing worries over tax revenues, and anxieties over whether the Duma will pass the 1997 budget, have given investors pause to assess their positions, especially after recent turbulence in the Kremlin.

"Now is a very turbulent time to own Russian assets -- prices are so high compared with where they were, and investors are trying to work out if Russia really deserves those levels," said Stuart Parkinson, debt analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
News that Russia's debut Eurobond was going ahead regardless was positive but not enough to salvage softer debt prices. But some investors remained bullish despite the turbulence.
"Despite the recent (IMF) set-back we still recommend Russia as a buy," ANZ Grindlays said in a research note.
POLAND too will draw investor attention as the government returns to parliament to try to pass the 1997 budget.
The focus will be in particular on its stock market, which has shed one or two points daily for the past five to six days amid debate over how much to cut taxes.
"Equities have been drifting off for the past week on the issue of loosening fiscal policy slightly, and on talk from the central bank about raising (interest) rates," Rendell said.

An IMF mission is due to visit BULGARIA this week, raising hopes there might be a chance the fund will release the long-delayed tranche of a standby loan that will haul the country back from the brink of default on its Brady debt.

Early results from Sunday's presidential elections suggest Bulgarians have thrown out the governing socialists in favour of opposition candidate Petar Stoyanov, but it is the outcome of the IMF mission that is dominating market attention.
"I'd love to recommend people buy Bulgaria, but it would be irresponsible," said one emerging debt analyst here, adding most players would steer clear until after the IMF loan materialises.
And next weekend ROMANIA holds parliamentary and presidential elections, while YUGOSLAVs vote in parliamentary polls.

Away from eastern Europe, MEXICO will remain in the spotlight as the peso weakness persists, hitting the stock market which fell to its lowest close this month on fears comapny earnings will suffer from higher interest rates.
The weakness pushed yields on Mexican 28-day T-bills last week to their highest levels since July 30, Foreign & Colonial Emerging Markets said.
But it added that the weaker currency may help attract foreign buyers into Mexican stocks.

CHILE's municipal elections, held on Sunday after a spate of strikes by teachers, bus drives, municipal workers and copper miners, have been widely tipped as a test of the political strength of President Eduardo Frei.
Results will be published during the week but political pundits widely tip Frei's Christian Democrat party to win a majority of local seats.
BRAZIL's $750 million five-year Eurobond issue will dominate that market this week as the country attempts to establish a non-Brady yield curve.
It will provide a welcome diversion from slow progress on constitutional reforms designed to reduce the country's fiscal deficit and anchor its inflation-beating Real plan securely.
Investors will also be watching how sentiment shapes up, ahead of November municipal elections, on amending the constitution to allow President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to be reelected.

In the Middle East, ISRAEL presents its 1997 budget on Tuesday with hefty cuts slated. Central bank governor Jacob Frenkel is due to announce interest rates for November this week, while investors will be looking for reform of Israel's capital markets and details of the country's hitherto stagnant privatisation programme.
An IMF team left TURKEY on the weekend and the government should signal soon whether it seeks to reach an accord with the Fund.
But U.S. payroll data for October, due for release on Friday, is likely to be the strongest influence on the Brady debt market as the Week progresses.
The IFC emerging market composite index of emerging market equities, denominated in dollars IFC/IPRD, was off 0.1 percent week on week at 297.21 points on Friday.
Latin America was off 1.2 percent at 534.14, Asia was off 0.9 percent at 252.62, and Europe, Middle East and Africa was quoted down 0.4 percent at 140.95.
